title: Advance Auto Parts Is (Finally) Getting What They Deserve…

sections.chapter: Advance Auto Parts, in the news
paras: On May 31st, 2023, Advance Auto Parts told its shareholders some bad news.
It cut its quarterly dividend from 1 dollar and 50 cents a share to just 25 cents.
The stock fell about 35 percent in a single day.
That September, S and P cut the company's debt rating to junk.
The same month, the CEO was gone.
In February 2024, Advance told regulators it couldn't file its annual report on time.
It had found errors in its own books.
And in November 2024, it announced it would close 523 of its stores.
Here's the strange part.
Americans are keeping their cars longer than ever, about 12.8 years on average.
Old cars need parts.
Its two biggest rivals, AutoZone and O'Reilly, are growing.
And Advance is shrinking.
This is the story of how the company that set out to be the biggest parts seller in North America fell behind, where the money in a parts store really comes from, and why the bill finally came due.

sections.chapter: The biggest parts store in America
paras: The story starts in 1932, in Roanoke, Virginia.
A man named Arthur Taubman takes over a small chain called Advance Stores.
Over the next eight decades, it grows into one of America's big parts chains.
Then, in October 2013, Advance makes the biggest bet in its history.
It agrees to buy General Parts International, the company behind Carquest, for 2.04 billion dollars in cash.
Advance says the deal creates the largest automotive aftermarket parts provider in North America.
When it closes in January 2014, the new Advance has about 5,300 company stores, another 1,400 independent Carquest stores, and more than 9.3 billion dollars in sales.
But bigger isn't the same as better.
Within two years, an activist investor, Starboard Value, takes a stake and gets seats on the board.
In 2016, Advance hires the head of Frito-Lay North America, Tom Greco, as its new CEO.
And for a moment, it looks like it worked.
In 2021, Advance's same store sales jumped 10.7 percent.
Sales hit 11 billion dollars.
The company celebrated the way public companies do.
It returned a record 1 billion dollars to shareholders that year, mostly by buying back its own stock.
Early in 2022, it raised its dividend by 50 percent, to 1 dollar and 50 cents a quarter.
In November 2021, the stock hit a record of about 242 dollars a share.

sections.chapter: How a parts store makes money
paras: To understand the fall, you need to understand the business.
A parts store has two very different customers.
The first one is you.
It's Saturday morning, your car won't start, and you walk in for a battery.
The industry calls you do it yourself.
The second customer is the repair shop down the road.
It has a car on the lift and a driver waiting in the lobby.
It needs a part, and it needs it in the next hour.
The industry calls that do it for me, or commercial.
At O'Reilly, the split is roughly half and half.
At AutoZone, the repair shops are about a third of its American sales, and the fastest growing part.
Now, follow one 100 dollar part.
At AutoZone and O'Reilly, the gross margin is about 52 percent.
So on that part, roughly 52 dollars are left after paying the supplier.
That's our illustration, using their reported margins.
Out of that 52 dollars come the rent, the wages, the delivery trucks and the warehouses.
At the two leaders, about 18 to 20 dollars of every 100 are left as operating profit.
For a store that sells brake pads and wiper blades, that is a remarkable number.
Here's the honest part.
None of these companies publish the margin on a do it yourself sale versus a repair shop sale.
AutoZone's finance chief has said the commercial mix drags its margin slightly, so the shop business is the lower margin one.
But it's the one that grows.
What really decides who wins is speed.
A normal AutoZone store carries 20 to 25 thousand different parts.
Its biggest hub stores carry up to 110 thousand.
If the shop calls and you have the part on a truck in 30 minutes, you get the next call too.
If you don't, they call someone else.
And the winners do something else with all that cash.
Since 1998, AutoZone has spent 40.5 billion dollars buying back its own shares.
Its share count has fallen by about 89 percent.
Fewer shares means every share left owns a bigger slice of the profit.
Fall number one was hiding in the warehouses.
When Advance bought Carquest, it got thousands of stores.
It also got a second supply chain, with its own warehouses and its own way of doing things.
Years later, the networks still hadn't been fully combined.
In February 2024, the new CEO, Shane O'Kelly, put it bluntly on a call with investors.
He said the network was inefficient and needed substantial work.
Advance and Carquest were running 38 distribution centers.
In his words, thirty-eight is far too many.
Think about what that means for the repair shop.
The part might exist somewhere in the system, but not in the right building.
So the truck doesn't come in 30 minutes, and the shop calls O'Reilly.
O'Kelly said it himself in November 2024.
The biggest gap to its rivals was sales at the store level.
The stores simply weren't selling as much as the stores across the street.

sections.chapter: Fall number two: the money and the books
paras: Fall number two is about where the money went.
In 2022, the boom faded.
Advance's same store sales grew just 0.3 percent.
But the payouts didn't slow down.
That year, Advance spent about 598 million dollars on buybacks and 336 million on dividends.
Add 2021, and by our math, it handed about 1.9 billion dollars to shareholders in two years, while its warehouses needed fixing.
Then came May 2023.
Advance cut its profit forecast for the year by about 40 percent.
It slashed the dividend it had raised just a year earlier.
And the stock lost about a third of its value in one day.
The fallout came fast.
Advance's debt was cut to junk.
The CEO and the finance chief left.
About 400 corporate jobs were cut.
Then the accounting.
In February 2024, Advance said it needed more time for its annual report.
It had found errors in its 2021 and 2022 results, mostly tied to product returns and credits from its suppliers.
The company called the errors immaterial.
But it also said its internal controls over its own reporting were not effective.
Investors sued, claiming they had been misled.
To be clear, those were allegations.
A federal judge dismissed the case in January 2025, and an appeals court upheld that decision.
But by then, activist investors had already won three seats on the board.
Fall number three is the shrink.
In August 2024, Advance agreed to sell Worldpac, its parts business for specialty and import cars, to the private equity firm Carlyle for 1.5 billion dollars.
Then, in November, came the closures.
523 Advance stores.
204 independent locations that carried its parts.
And four distribution centers.
In the quarter before, its adjusted operating margin was 0.8 percent.
That's less than a dollar of profit on every 100 dollars of sales.
How many people lost their jobs?
We looked, and Advance never published a national number.
In Texas alone, state notices listed 143 jobs.
In 2025, Advance closed 522 stores and opened 39.
Sales were 8.6 billion dollars.
Three years earlier, they were 11.2 billion.
Part of that is the Worldpac sale, but not all of it.
That July, both S and P and Moody's cut its rating again.
And the comeback keeps slipping.
In February 2026, O'Kelly said the company was on pace to fall short of its 7 percent margin target for 2027.
In August, the stock dropped 21 percent in a day after sales missed expectations.
Here's the gap today.
In the third quarter of 2026, O'Reilly's same store sales grew 7.2 percent.
Advance's fell 1.2 percent.
On November 25th, its stock closed at about 46 dollars.
That's roughly 81 percent below its record.
Now, the other side, because it matters.
Advance is not going out of business.
It still has about 4,300 stores and close to 800 independent partners.
It expects about 8.5 billion dollars in sales this year, and it had more than 3 billion dollars in cash at the end of its latest quarter.
The repair work is real, too.
Its 38 distribution centers are down to 16.
It's opening what it calls market hubs, bigger stores that stock far more parts nearby.
It had 35 of them by June 2026, and wants 60 by 2027.
Its adjusted operating margin was back up to 4.5 percent last quarter.
And the rivals have had help.
In May 2025, a 25 percent tariff on imported auto parts took effect, and prices went up across the industry.
AutoZone said prices on the very same parts were up just over 7 percent.
Some of its 2026 profit also came from tariff refunds.
Not every gain at the top was earned on the shop floor.
And Advance isn't the first parts chain to stumble.
Pep Boys was once a household name in American car care.
Carl Icahn's company bought it about a decade ago, for roughly 1 billion dollars, after a bidding war.
Its parts distribution business, Auto Plus, filed for bankruptcy in January 2023.
By early 2025, Icahn was out of the parts business entirely.
And in August 2026, Pep Boys itself was sold to Mavis, the tire chain, for 700 million dollars.
Even NAPA is being reshaped.
Its parent, Genuine Parts, plans to split into two public companies in early 2027.
Bloomberg reported that O'Reilly showed interest in the NAPA business, but Genuine Parts denied talks with any competitor.
The lesson is simple.
In auto parts, the big don't automatically survive.
The fast ones do.

sections.chapter: So, did they get what they deserve?
paras: So, is Advance Auto Parts finally getting what it deserves?
In a lot of ways, yes.
It bought its way to the top, never fully fixed the machine behind the stores, and paid out almost 2 billion dollars while the warehouses waited.
Then it found errors in its own books.
The market didn't fail Advance.
The same old cars, the same repair shops and the same rising prices made AutoZone and O'Reilly richer than ever.
Advance had the same customers, and lost them to the store across the street.
Here's the number that sums it up.
Last quarter, O'Reilly kept about 21 dollars of operating profit on every 100 dollars of sales.
Advance kept about 2 dollars, or 4 and a half on an adjusted basis.
In this business, the part isn't really the product.
The product is the 30 minutes it takes to get it to you.
